semantics.note: The normalised claim matches what he said: Bing said the images were original, and that was untrue because they resembled DC characters.

contract.note: Requiring an independent record of the exchange and the images is fair. The ambiguity flag about how 'original' is judged is noted but does not drive the result here.

reviews.rationale: The packet has no evidence items. The only record of the exchange is the authors' own screenshots, which cannot prove the claim. No independent report or archive was found, so the evidence available by the cutoff neither supports nor contradicts the claim.

attribution.note: These are the post's own words, which Marcus co-authored and endorses.

semantics.note: This is a firm, universal claim about all guardrails up to the post. 'Thus far' is kept. The 'virtually any' framing sits in the premise; the claim itself is 'none'.

contract.note: He named no measure. Reading 'effective' as a practically useful balance, not perfection, is ordinary and fair. Without a threshold, though, the result depends on how broad the evaluations must be.

evidence.note: Dated before the post. Shows broad transferable jailbreaks against ChatGPT, Bard and Claude, but measures no benign-request refusals, so it covers only one side of the balance.
XSTest (Oct 2023) found GPT-4 handled safe and unsafe prompts well. That cuts against a universal failure claim, but there was no adversarial testing, so it misses the contradiction bar.
SmoothLLM cut GCG attack success sharply while keeping QA performance, but PAIR still succeeded about 50% of the time and refusals were not measured directly. The result is mixed.

reviews.rationale: Neither condition is met. No representative evaluation shows that every guardrail failed. The positive results (GPT-4 on XSTest, SmoothLLM) each lack either adversarial coverage or a direct measure of benign refusals, while e1 shows real permissiveness failures. The packet does not settle the universal claim.

attribution.note: These are the post's own words, co-authored and endorsed by Marcus.

semantics.note: The claim about OpenAI's position is firm. 'Apparently' qualifies only the not-paying part and is kept. Reading 'license any other data' as licensing all non-public-domain data fits the context.

contract.note: Reading the claim as unwillingness to train only on public-domain or licensed data, rather than refusing all licensing, is the ordinary reading in context and is fair. The stronger reading would be undercut by e2.

evidence.note: OpenAI's own Jan 8, 2024 post claims training on public internet material is fair use. That is its stated policy, which is exactly what is assessed. It is a company disclosure, but the claim is about OpenAI's own position.
The Axel Springer deal (Dec 2023) shows OpenAI licensed some content. It does not show a policy of licensing everything, so it qualifies the claim without contradicting it.

reviews.rationale: Just before the post, OpenAI publicly said its training on copyrighted internet material relies on fair use, a legal basis that needs no paid licences. Selective licensing such as Axel Springer does not amount to committing to train only on public-domain or licensed data. The support condition is met.

attribution.note: These are the post's own words, co-authored and endorsed by Marcus.

semantics.note: A firm causal claim ('would be'). The drafter's 'could' modality understates it slightly, but the normalised proposition still says 'would decisively address'.

contract.note: Reading 'the problem' as copyright liability is fair, since the context is about infringement claims. That a licence must also cover output use is the evaluator's inference, not something he stated.

evidence.note: UK IPO guidance says works out of copyright are free to use. This backs the public-domain route, though applying it to AI training is an inference.
UK IPO guidance says a licence sets out what the user may do. This backs the licensing route, as long as the licence covers the relevant uses.

reviews.rationale: Official guidance confirms that public-domain works are free to use and that licences authorise the uses they cover. Under the contract's reading, both routes remove the copyright objection. Nothing in the packet shows infringement despite public-domain status or a valid licence. The licensing route holds only if the licence covers output use.
